Class Panel

java.lang.Object
com.trevlar.menukit.api.panel.Panel
public class Panel extends Object
The basic unit of composition. Every element in MenuKit lives inside a Panel, because the panel is what shows and hides, and showing and hiding is what makes menus dynamic.

A Panel holds an ordered list of PanelElements (buttons, text labels, anything implementing the interface), plus a style, a position, a toggle key and a visibility flag. Visibility can change; the element list is fixed once built.

The same Panel type is used in inventory menus, on the HUD and on standalone screens. What is specific to each (slot groups, HUD anchoring, a standalone screen's lifecycle) lives in whatever holds the panel, not in the panel.

A Panel is client-only: it is how a panel looks. On a MenuKit: Containers custom menu the server's half of a panel (its id, its slot groups, whether it is shown) belongs to the menu; the screen builds a Panel for each and shows it while the server says so.

Visibility: imperative or supplier-driven

Panel visibility can be controlled two ways:
  • Imperative via setVisible(boolean). The Panel holds the boolean.
  • Supplier-driven via visibleWhen(java.util.function.BooleanSupplier). Consumer holds the state; Panel reads via the supplier on each isVisible() call. The usual choice for injected panels, HUDs and standalone screens, like a Toggle's state(get, set).
Only one applies at a time; see visibleWhen(java.util.function.BooleanSupplier) for which wins.

      @Internal public Panel(String id, List<PanelElement> elements, boolean visible, PanelStyle style, PanelPosition position, int toggleKey)

      elements - panel elements, buttons, text labels, etc. (immutable after construction)

    • interiorPadding

      public int interiorPadding()
      The padding, in pixels, between the panel's outer (background) bounds and where its elements start.
      • PanelStyle.NONE: 0. With no visible frame, the element edge is the panel edge, and hover, click and tooltip bounds match the elements.
      • Every other style (PanelStyle.RAISED, PanelStyle.DARK, PanelStyle.INSET): INTERIOR_PADDING (7), room between the visible frame and the elements.

      Used wherever outer bounds are worked out from the elements or the other way round: MKScreen, CustomContainerScreen, and the default-padding constructors of ScreenPanelAdapter and SlotGroupPanelAdapter. The explicit-padding constructors use the padding they are given.

    • getElements

      public List<PanelElement> getElements()
      The elements to lay out, render and send input to.

      Usually the panel's own elements. When the content is taller than the panel's viewport (a pinned height, or the room the screen leaves), this is a single internal ScrollContainer holding them, which passes render, clicks, scrolling and releases on to its children. To the screen it is just another element.

      ScrollContainer also passes onAttach, onDetach and keyPressed on, so widget-wrapping elements (Slider, TextField) inside a scrolling panel still register their vanilla widgets and get key input.

    • size

      public Panel size(int w, int h)
      Pins this panel's width and height, overriding the size getWidth() and getHeight() would compute from the elements. Use it when the content is supplier-driven and its size would change from frame to frame, so the panels stacked after it in the same region don't jump. Text wraps to the pinned width and content taller than the pinned height scrolls.
      Parameters:
      w - pinned width in pixels (must be non-negative)
      h - pinned height in pixels (must be non-negative)
      Returns:
      this panel, for method chaining

    • setAvailableContentWidth

      @Internal public void setAvailableContentWidth(int avail)
      Sets the content width the screen leaves this panel. PanelHost calls it every frame, before getWidth(), with the room left before the screen-edge margin at the panel's anchor. An unpinned panel whose content is wider wraps its TextLabels to it (and sizes a scroll viewport to it) instead of running off the screen, so every panel wraps at the screen edge without opting in.

      Only a changed value marks the configuration dirty and drops the scroll container. Since this runs every frame, it would otherwise either keep a stale wrap or rebuild the scroll container each frame, resetting its drag state. A window resize re-fits; a stable frame costs nothing.

      Internal: it carries screen geometry the panel itself doesn't know. Values below a small minimum are raised to it, so a degenerate frame can't wrap to zero.

      Parameters:
      avail - content-width room before the screen-edge margin, in pixels

    • setAvailableContentHeight

      @Internal public void setAvailableContentHeight(int avail)
      Sets the content height the screen leaves this panel, the height counterpart of setAvailableContentWidth(int). PanelHost works out the room the panel's anchor leaves toward the screen edge (RegionMath.availableMenuHeight(OutsideRegion, Reference, int, int)); when the content is taller, the panel scrolls within it (the same ScrollContainer as pinnedHeight) instead of running off the screen. Content that fits is unaffected: no scrolling, no scrollbar room.

      Like setAvailableContentWidth(int), only a changed value triggers a reconfigure. Internal.

      Parameters:
      avail - content-height room before the screen-edge margin, in pixels

    • setFrameHeight

      @Internal public void setFrameHeight(int height)
      Sets the frame band: the content height from the panel's content top down to where the frame beside it ends, or -1 when no frame is beside it. The host feeds it every frame, before measuring, for a panel in a side region (RIGHT_ALIGN_*, LEFT_ALIGN_*) on a container screen, on a slot group (whose frame is still the container screen's) and beside a standalone screen's main panel; every other placement gets -1. Each element receives it as its wrap height (PanelElement.wrapHeight(int)).

      Not a scroll ceiling: a panel taller than its band does not scroll (that is setAvailableContentHeight(int), at the screen's edge). Like those, it only re-lays out when the value changes. Internal.

      Parameters:
      height - content-height room down to the frame's bottom, or -1

    • setScreenKind

      @Internal public void setScreenKind(ScreenKind kind)
      The kind of screen the panel is on, fed by its host before each layout (the host fixes it from its screen, ScreenKind.of(Screen)). An auto-scrolling panel on an options screen lays its elements out inside the list band's inset (ScrollContainer.viewportWidthFor(int, ScreenKind)). Re-lays out only when it changes, like the size limits. Internal.

    • setVisible

      public void setVisible(boolean visible)
      Sets this panel's visibility.

      Ignored while a supplier is set. After visibleWhen(java.util.function.BooleanSupplier) with a non-null supplier, the supplier alone decides, so unrelated code can't override it. Call visibleWhen(null) first to go back to setVisible.

    • visibleWhen

      public Panel visibleWhen(@Nullable BooleanSupplier supplier)
      Makes a supplier decide this panel's visibility. isVisible() reads it on every call and setVisible(boolean) is ignored.

      Like an element's state(get, set): you hold the state and MenuKit reads it, so there is no second copy to fall out of sync.

      Precedence

      • Calling visibleWhen(supplier) replaces any prior setVisible(boolean) state. The imperative visible field is ignored while the supplier is active.
      • To go back to setVisible, call visibleWhen(null). The prior setVisible state is not restored; visibility resets to the default (true) until the consumer calls setVisible again.

      Sync

      A panel's visibility is a client-side rendering decision. Where it must drive slot inertness and sync (a MenuKit: Containers custom menu), the menu holds it on the server and the screen reads it through this supplier.
      Parameters:
      supplier - the visibility condition, or null to go back to setVisible.
      Returns:
      this panel, for method chaining.

    • disabledWhen

      public Panel disabledWhen(@Nullable BooleanSupplier condition)
      Disables the whole panel while condition holds, read every frame (pass null to clear). Every element draws its disabled look (text and section headers grey, controls dark) and takes no clicks, wheel or keys; containers pass it down to their children. The panel itself stays present: it still claims its area, so nothing behind it reacts either.

    • isDisabled

    • opaque

      public Panel opaque(boolean isOpaque)
      Sets whether this panel takes all input over its bounds.

      When true and the panel is visible, input inside its bounding box (clicks, hover, tooltips) goes to the panel and never reaches vanilla widgets underneath. Empty space in the panel eats input, tooltips for items behind it are suppressed, and slot hover returns null. Clicks never pass through a visible panel unless it opts out, as transparent overlays do.

      The claim rule: an opaque panel claims its whole bounding box, regardless of PanelStyle, with no holes; a transparent panel (opaque(false)) claims only its solid elements (shown, opaque, interactive). PanelStyle.NONE + opaque(true) is the "click blocker" pattern (invisible but blocks input). A panel's own slots stay live under its own claim.

      Every host: panels on container and vanilla screens, slot-group panels, and a standalone screen's own panels all claim by this rule.

      Default: true.

      Parameters:
      isOpaque - true to make this panel interaction-opaque
      Returns:
      this panel, for chaining

    • isOpaque

    • dimsBehind

      public Panel dimsBehind(boolean dims)
      Sets whether the screen dims behind this panel while it is visible.

      When true and the panel is visible, a translucent black fill is drawn over the screen before this panel. Modal dialogs use it to stand apart from ordinary decoration.

      Independent of opaque(boolean): a panel can be opaque without dimming (popovers, dropdowns), or in principle transparent with a dim. Independent of tracksAsModal(boolean) too: the dim is only visual, while modal tracking governs the cursor and keyboard.

      Default: false.

      Parameters:
      dims - true to dim the screen behind this panel
      Returns:
      this panel, for chaining

    • dimsBehind

      public boolean dimsBehind()

    • tracksAsModal

      public Panel tracksAsModal(boolean tracks)
      Sets whether this panel acts as a modal for the whole window.

      When true and the panel is visible:

      • Cursor lock: Window.setAllowCursorChanges(false) every tick, so the cursor stays DEFAULT whatever vanilla widgets ask for (creative tabs and so on).
      • Keys: keys the panels don't take never reach the screen underneath. Escape runs the panel's onEscape(Runnable) action instead of closing the screen.
      • Clicks anywhere: a visible modal claims every point, so clicks outside it are eaten too.

      Pointer-based suppression (slot hover, tooltips) comes from opaque(boolean) within the panel's bounds and doesn't need tracksAsModal. The pointer has a position, so that can be local; the cursor shape and keyboard belong to the whole window, so only modals take them over.

      Default: false.

      Parameters:
      tracks - true to participate in modal tracking
      Returns:
      this panel, for chaining

    • tracksAsModal

      public boolean tracksAsModal()
      Whether this panel acts as a modal. See tracksAsModal(boolean).

    • isOverlayPositioned

      public boolean isOverlayPositioned()
      Whether this panel is a screen-centred overlay rather than part of the normal layout: true when it declares PanelPosition.center(), or is dimsBehind() or tracksAsModal().

      Hosts use this one check for three things: centring the panel on the screen, leaving it out of the normal layout, and drawing it in the overlay layer on top. Counting dimsBehind and tracksAsModal means a dialog made with modal() is centred without calling center(), while a non-dim, non-modal overlay opts in with position(PanelPosition.center()).

      This is about position only. The dim is still drawn only for dimsBehind(), so an overlay can be centred on top without dimming.

    • isPopover

      public boolean isPopover()
      Whether this panel is a popover (Panel.Builder.popover()): it draws and claims above every ordinary panel on the screen, below the modal overlay.

    • modal

      public Panel modal()
      Sets all three modal flags, the same as opaque(true).dimsBehind(true).tracksAsModal(true): a real modal in one call. Popovers, dropdowns and click blockers use the separate setters.

      Undefined: opaque(false) with tracksAsModal(true) makes no sense (clicks pass through while the cursor and keys are locked) and is almost certainly a bug. It isn't rejected, but its behaviour is not defined.

      Returns:
      this panel, for chaining

    • onEscape

      public Panel onEscape(@Nullable Runnable action)
      Sets the action run when the player presses Escape while this panel is the topmost visible modal. The host (MKScreen, or the key listener for injected panels) runs it and eats the key, so Escape dismisses the modal instead of closing the screen under it.

      The dialog builders set it for you: ConfirmDialog to its onCancel and AlertDialog to its onAcknowledge, so Escape does what the button does. For a modal you build yourself, pass your dismiss callback here.

      Without an action, a visible tracksAsModal panel still makes the host eat Escape, so it can't close the screen.

      Parameters:
      action - the dismiss callback, or null to clear it
      Returns:
      this panel, for chaining

    • getEscapeAction

    • tooltip

      public Panel tooltip(net.minecraft.network.chat.Component text)
      Sets a tooltip shown whenever the cursor is over the panel's outer bounds, say to explain what a collapsible or configurable panel is for.

      For tooltips on specific children, put them on the children. Child tooltips are queued while the elements render and the panel's after, and the last one queued wins, so over a child with both, the panel's shows.

    • maybeQueueTooltip

      public void maybeQueueTooltip(net.minecraft.client.gui.GuiGraphicsExtractor graphics, int panelX, int panelY, int panelWidth, int panelHeight, int mouseX, int mouseY, boolean hasMouseInput)
      Queues the panel's tooltip, if it has one, when the cursor is inside the given outer rectangle. The host calls it after rendering the elements.

      Skipped when hasMouseInput is false. The HUD passes mouseX = -1, which would miss the hit test anyway; the check makes that explicit and saves the supplier call.
